speaker: April Dunford
title: How to nail your product positioning | April Dunford (Obviously Awesome)
question: In growing B2B software companies, is weak product positioning usually caused by not having the right positioning or by internal misalignment?
guest: I would say the majority of the time it's misalignment, because a piece of the company has it right, and the other pieces don't. I usually see one of two things happening. Sometimes a founder comes to me and says, "I know exactly how to tell this story—put me in front of a customer and I crush it every time. But we've gotten big now, I hired a new VP of marketing, a new VP of sales, and a product leader, and they don't understand it the way I do. When I listen to a sales call or look at our marketing, it's all wrong, and I can't get everybody aligned." The other case is the opposite. A founder used to run all the deals and knew the market cold, then the company grew fast and hired senior leaders, while the market itself shifted. Then the head of product or marketing says, "We're positioned for what the market used to be, and I can't get the founder's head around it." Sales sees what's happening in sales, marketing sees marketing, product sees the product, and the founder only gets pulled into certain deals—so everyone has pieces of the truth, but no alignment.

points.core: Internal misalignment causes most positioning breakdowns in scaling B2B companies.
points.note: Accept: the majority of positioning problems stem from unaligned teams where one part of the company already has it right. Do not credit: both-sides hedging claiming both causes are equally common without identifying misalignment as dominant.

points.core: Founder-led sales knowledge often fails to transfer to newly hired executives.
points.note: Accept: a founder can still pitch and close deals effectively, but newly hired VPs of marketing, sales, or product execute a different story. Do not credit: generic complaints about poor onboarding or bad executive hires.

points.core: Founders removed from daily deals often stay anchored to outdated markets.
points.note: Accept: the market shifts during rapid growth while the founder only joins select deals and holds onto legacy positioning that product or marketing leaders know is stale. Do not credit: generic statements that markets change over time.

points.core: Different departments form conflicting positioning views from seeing separate slices of reality.
points.note: Accept: sales, marketing, product, and founders each observe different customer signals, creating partial truths that never reconcile without cross-functional alignment. Do not credit: vague advice to communicate better without citing asymmetric departmental visibility.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
More often it's internal misalignment, though the two are tangled together, and there's no rigorous data settling the question; this is practitioner consensus rather than a measured finding.

In growing B2B software companies, someone usually has a reasonable positioning in their head, often the founder. The problem is that it was never made explicit or agreed on. As the company scales, sales pitches one thing, marketing writes another, product builds toward a third, and each team holds a different answer to "who is this for, and what do we replace?" The market experiences this as weak positioning, even if any single version would have worked. April Dunford, probably the best-known positioning practitioner, makes this argument and treats positioning as a cross-functional exercise for that reason: a positioning statement written by marketing alone rarely sticks.

That said, misalignment is sometimes a symptom, not a cause. If the product has drifted, added segments, or the market shifted, teams diverge because the old positioning stopped fitting reality.

A quick test: ask five leaders separately to name the target customer and main competitive alternative. Divergent answers mean alignment; consistent but ineffective answers mean the positioning itself is wrong.

models.answer: In growing B2B software companies, weak product positioning is usually caused by internal misalignment rather than not having the right positioning available. Because a growing company already has paying customers and proven traction, the core ingredients of strong positioning—real competitive alternatives, differentiated capabilities, and clear customer value—almost always exist inside the business. The problem emerges as the company scales and teams view the product through competing lenses: sales pitches whatever closes this quarter's deals, product sells the future roadmap, and founders pitch a broad investor vision. Rather than making hard trade-offs about which target buyers and use cases to prioritize, leadership often defaults to consensus. That compromise produces vague, watered-down messaging broad enough to satisfy every executive internally, yet too generic to resonate with buyers. Even when marketing defines sharp positioning on paper, it fails in practice if sales, product, and leadership do not commit to it. While shifting markets or new product lines can genuinely outdate earlier positioning, internal misalignment is usually what creates and sustains weak positioning.

noweb.answer:
In growing B2B software companies, weak positioning is usually caused by internal misalignment rather than an inability to figure out the right positioning—though the first directly creates the second. Early traction often comes from opportunistic deals across varied buyers. As the company scales, teams form competing views of the business: sales pitches whatever closes the current deal, product builds toward an expansive future vision, and leadership resists narrowing the target market for fear of leaving revenue behind. Caught in the middle, marketing defaults to vague, catch-all messaging that satisfies every internal stakeholder while resonating with no buyer.

Most growing companies already hold the customer insights needed to craft strong positioning. What they lack is executive agreement on who the best-fit customer is, what competitive alternative they replace, and which segments they are willing to deprioritize. Even sharp positioning on paper quickly unravels if sales, product, and leadership do not commit to the same trade-offs. Ultimately, weak positioning at this stage is rarely a market-research or copywriting failure; it is an unresolved strategy argument made public.

In growing B2B software companies, weak positioning usually comes from internal misalignment more than from never having found the right positioning. The two are related, though, because misalignment is often how a missing or outdated positioning shows up.

Practitioners like April Dunford say the same thing. Most teams have a decent positioning somewhere. The founders know it, or the best salespeople use it in deals. The problem is that it was never made explicit, agreed on, and adopted across the company. As a company grows, product, sales, marketing and leadership each build their own version. Product describes features, sales tells whatever story closes deals, and marketing chases a category. Customers then get mixed messages, which looks like "weak positioning."

Growth also wears positioning down. The product grows, new segments come in, and the original story stops fitting, but nobody is clearly responsible for updating it.

So the fix is rarely a better tagline. Teams need a cross-functional process to agree on the best-fit customers, the real competitive alternatives, and the differentiated value. Then sales materials, the roadmap, and messaging all need to follow from that agreement.

noweb.answer: In growing B2B software companies, weak product positioning is usually caused more by internal misalignment than by a failure to find the right positioning in the abstract. Early on, founders often have an intuitive, effective story, but as the company scales—adding features, moving upmarket, or chasing adjacent segments—product, marketing, sales, and leadership begin emphasizing different audiences and value propositions. Even when a team crafts strong positioning on paper, it breaks down in practice if sales pitches a broader use case to hit quota, product builds for a different persona, and marketing speaks to a third. Conversely, when a company genuinely lacks clear positioning, the underlying reason is almost always organizational: leadership has avoided making and enforcing the hard trade-offs about who the product is for, what it replaces, and why it wins. Finding the right positioning matters, of course, but in scaling B2B organizations, weak positioning is most often an alignment and decision-making problem rather than a messaging one.

In a growing B2B software company, internal misalignment is often the first thing to investigate. Marketing may describe the product for one buyer, sales may win deals with another, and product may build for a third. From the outside, that looks like weak positioning even if one team has found a message that resonates.

Ask leaders in each function, independently, who buys the product, what those buyers would do without it, and why they choose it. Then compare their answers with what buyers say about recent deals. If one team’s account fits the evidence and the others tell different stories, alignment is the likely issue. If everyone agrees but buyers give a different reason for choosing you, the positioning itself needs work. Both problems can coexist.
